info.name: Anthropic Messages API — Learning Collection
info.description:
Hands-on tour of POST /v1/messages: response assembly, streaming, tool use (single, chained, parallel), errors, caching, and token counting.

Setup: import the companion environment, set `apiKey` (secret), then run the folders top to bottom. Several requests chain — the tool-use requests write variables that the next request consumes, so run them in order the first time.

exec: console.warn('apiKey is empty — set it in the environment before running.');
// Shared helpers available to every request's own tests.
// (Postman runs collection-level tests after request-level ones,
//  so these assertions apply to all JSON responses.)
// content is an ARRAY of blocks, not a string. Concatenate every
// block whose type is 'text'. Blocks of other types (thinking,
// tool_use) live in the same array and must be skipped.

request.description: The smallest valid request. Note what comes back: `content` is an array of blocks, `stop_reason` tells you why generation ended, and `usage` reports the token split. Open the Console (Ctrl/Cmd+Alt+C) to see the assembled text the test script builds.

The API is stateless: there is no conversation ID. "Memory" is just you resending the full `messages` array, alternating user/assistant. Delete the middle two entries and Claude no longer knows the name.

exec: // Postman shows the raw SSE stream. Same assembly problem as 1.1,
// but one delta at a time: content_block_delta events carry
// text_delta fragments that you concatenate per block index.
let e; try { e = JSON.parse(line); } catch (err) { return; }

request.description:
Add `"stream": true` and the same endpoint returns text/event-stream. The event sequence is: message_start → (content_block_start → content_block_delta* → content_block_stop)* → message_delta (carries the final stop_reason and output token count) → message_stop.

The console log shows the text rebuilt from the deltas — that's exactly what an SDK's stream helper does for you.

Same body shape as /v1/messages, minus `max_tokens`. Free, no generation. Add the `tools` array from folder 3 and re-run to see how much your tool schemas cost on every single request — that's the usual surprise.
Live list of model IDs available to your key, with context window and output caps. Use this instead of hardcoding IDs from memory.

item.name: 2.1 Narrate, then call (text + tool_use in one response)

request.description: This is why `content` is an array. One assistant turn holds a `text` block AND a `tool_use` block. Naive code that does `content[0].text` works here by luck and breaks the moment the order flips — always filter by `type`.

A third block type: `thinking`, which arrives before the `text` block. Shown here with the `budget_tokens` form because this collection defaults to claude-haiku-4-5.

On Claude Opus 5 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 4.6+ this form is REJECTED with a 400 — those models use `"thinking": {"type": "adaptive", "display": "summarized"}` plus `"output_config": {"effort": "high"}` instead. Swap `model` to `claude-opus-5` and try both bodies to see the error — a useful thing to have felt once.
HTTP 200, valid JSON, sentence cut mid-word. This failure is silent unless you check `stop_reason` — the single most common bug in first-draft API code.

exec: // Build the follow-up messages array for request 3.2.
// Rule: echo the assistant turn back VERBATIM (all blocks), then send
// a user turn whose content is the tool_result blocks.
const fakeWeather = { Austin: '97F, sunny', Denver: '58F, snow flurries', Miami: '88F, thunderstorms' };
{ role: 'user', content: "What's the weather in Austin?" },

request.description: Claude does NOT run your tool. It returns a `tool_use` block — an intent — and stops with `stop_reason: "tool_use"`. The test script executes a fake weather lookup and stashes the follow-up conversation in a collection variable. Run 3.2 next.

exec: throw new Error('Run 3.1 first — it populates singleToolMessages.');

request.description:
The `messages` array is injected from 3.1. Three things must hold or you get a 400:
1. The assistant turn is echoed back with its blocks intact.
2. `tool_use_id` matches exactly.
3. `tools` is still declared on this request — tool definitions are per-request, not remembered.

Try breaking each one on purpose. The error messages are worth reading.

item.name: 3.3 Parallel tool calls → capture all ids

exec: calls.forEach(c => console.log('  ' + c.name + ' ' + JSON.stringify(c.input) + '  id=' + c.id));
pm.test('more than one tool_use block', () => pm.expect(calls.length).to.be.above(1));
const weather = { Austin: '97F, sunny', Denver: '58F, snow flurries', Miami: '88F, thunderstorms' };
const times   = { Austin: '3:42 PM CDT (UTC-5)', Denver: '2:42 PM MDT (UTC-6)', Miami: '4:42 PM EDT (UTC-4)' };
// KEY RULE: every tool_result goes in ONE user message.
{ role: 'user', content: 'Compare the current weather in Austin, Denver, and Miami.' },

request.description:
One assistant turn, three `tool_use` blocks. Your job is to run them concurrently and return all three results together.

Flip `disable_parallel_tool_use` to `true` and re-run: you get one call per turn instead, which costs three round trips for the same answer.

item.name: 3.4 Return ALL tool_results in one user message

exec: throw new Error('Run 3.3 first — it populates parallelToolMessages.');

request.description: All N `tool_result` blocks ride in a SINGLE user message. Splitting them across several user messages is accepted by the API but quietly teaches the model to stop batching calls — and it's the bug you'd never find from a stack trace.

The question has nothing to do with weather, but `tool_choice: {type: "tool"}` forces the call anyway — watch what it invents for `city`. This is the structured-extraction trick (force a tool whose schema is your output shape) and also a caution: forcing removes Claude's judgment.

Other values: `{"type":"any"}` (must use some tool), `{"type":"auto"}` (default), `{"type":"none"}`.

exec: console.log('Did it retry with a tool_use block? ' + body.content.some(b => b.type === 'tool_use'));

request.description:
Hand-written history with a synthetic tool_use id — proof that the API only checks that ids match within the request, not that it issued them.

Return failures as `tool_result` with `is_error: true` rather than dropping the block or throwing. Claude reads the error text and decides whether to retry, try a different city spelling, or tell the user. Dropping the block is a 400.
Error envelope shape: `{"type":"error","error":{"type":"authentication_error","message":"..."}}`. Every failure uses this shape — branch on `error.type`, not on the message string.
Also what a hallucinated date-suffixed model ID looks like from the server's side.
`max_tokens` is required on /v1/messages (and only there — count_tokens doesn't take it). Note how the validation error points at the exact field path.

Nothing special about the body — look at the Headers tab and the console. `request-id` is what you quote in a support ticket; the ratelimit headers are what a production client should watch to back off *before* it gets a 429.

First call writes the cache: `cache_creation_input_tokens` is non-zero, `cache_read_input_tokens` is 0. Caching is a PREFIX match with a ~1024-token minimum, which is why the policy text is repeated — a short system prompt silently won't cache at all.

exec: console.log('If this failed: the system text differs from 5.1 by at least one byte, it is under ~1024 tokens, or the 5-minute TTL expired.');

request.description: Identical system prefix, different question → `cache_read_input_tokens` is non-zero at ~10% of the cost. Now go edit ONE character in the system text and re-run: the hit disappears. That single experiment explains most "why is my cache hit rate zero" bugs (a timestamp or UUID in the prompt).
